section.title: He Heals the Brokenhearted
section.sectionRationale: The second Hallelujah psalm, grouped in three stanzas. It celebrates the LORD who rebuilds Jerusalem and gathers the exiles, heals the brokenhearted, numbers and names every star, sustains creation, and sends forth His word to Jacob, a word later shown to be made flesh, John 1:14.
section.thesis: The same LORD whose power numbers and names every star stoops to heal the shattered heart, provide for all creation, and speak His word to His people, a word that becomes flesh in Jesus Christ.
section.frameNote: Three stanzas, each opening with a summons to praise: the LORD who restores Jerusalem and heals the brokenhearted, verses 1-6; the LORD who sustains creation and delights in those who fear Him, verses 7-11; and the LORD whose word runs swiftly and is declared uniquely to Israel, verses 12-20.

units.label: It is good to sing praises
units.note: the LORD restores Jerusalem and heals the brokenhearted

verses.text: {{haleluyah|Hallelujah}}! How good it is to sing praises to our God, how pleasant and lovely to praise Him!
The LORD builds up Jerusalem; He gathers the exiles of Israel.
He heals the {{nishberei-lev|brokenhearted}} and binds up their wounds.
He determines the number of the stars; He calls them each by name.
Great is our Lord, and mighty in power; His understanding has no limit.
The LORD sustains the humble, but casts the wicked to the ground.

units.label: Sing to the Lord with thanksgiving
units.note: the LORD sustains creation and delights in those who fear Him

verses.text: Sing to the LORD with thanksgiving; make music on the harp to our God,
who covers the sky with clouds, who prepares rain for the earth, who makes grass to grow on the hills.
He provides food for the animals, and for the young ravens when they call.
He does not delight in the strength of the horse; He takes no pleasure in the legs of a man.
The LORD is pleased with those who fear Him, who hope in His {{hesed|loving devotion}}.

units.label: He declares His word to Jacob
units.note: the LORD's provision, command over nature, and His word to Israel

verses.text: Exalt the LORD, O Jerusalem; praise your God, O Zion!
For He strengthens the bars of your gates and blesses the children within you.
He makes peace at your borders; He fills you with the finest wheat.
He sends forth His command to the earth; His {{davar|word}} runs swiftly.
He spreads the snow like wool; He scatters the frost like ashes;
He casts forth His hail like pebbles. Who can withstand His icy blast?
He sends forth His word and melts them; He unleashes His winds, and the waters flow.
He declares His word to Jacob, His statutes and judgments to Israel.
He has done this for no other nation; they do not know His judgments. {{haleluyah|Hallelujah}}!

haleluyah.gloss: An imperative call, praise the LORD. It opens and closes each of the last five psalms of the Psalter, framing the whole collection's final movement as one continuous shout of praise.

nishberei-lev.gloss: Shattered of heart, brokenhearted. The same LORD who numbers and names every star, a display of cosmic power beyond calculation, stoops to heal the shattered heart, an intimate compassion within that same power.

hesed.gloss: Covenant loving devotion, or steadfast love. The LORD delights not in human strength but in those who fear Him and hope in His hesed.

davar.gloss: Word, command, or matter. The LORD's davar governs weather and nations alike, running swiftly to accomplish His will, a word that becomes flesh in John's Gospel.

basic.context: This psalm celebrates the LORD's twin greatness, His cosmic power over the stars and the weather, and His intimate compassion for the brokenhearted and the humble. It moves through three stanzas, each opening with a summons to praise, and closes by noting Israel's unique privilege of receiving God's own word and statutes.
basic.hermeneutics: This is a hymn of praise for God's providential care, historically tied to the LORD rebuilding Jerusalem and gathering the exiles after the Babylonian captivity, but its abiding pattern is trust in the God whose vast power and tender compassion are never in tension.
basic.originalLanguages: The psalm frames its praise with haleluyah, praise the LORD. Verse 3 names the nishberei lev, the brokenhearted, whom God heals. Verse 11 grounds His delight in those who hope in His hesed, covenant love. Verses 15, 18, and 19 speak of His davar, word, running swiftly and being declared uniquely to Jacob.
basic.typology: The LORD who heals the brokenhearted, verse 3, anticipates Jesus, who reads Isaiah 61's promise of healing for the brokenhearted as His own mission, Luke 4:18. The LORD's word that runs swiftly and melts the frost, verses 15-18, anticipates the Word who was with God and was God, and who became flesh, John 1:1-14.
basic.christ: The healer of the brokenhearted, verse 3, and the LORD whose word runs swiftly and accomplishes His will, verses 15-19, are fulfilled in Jesus Christ, the Word made flesh, John 1:14, who heals the brokenhearted, Luke 4:18, and whose word is living and active, Hebrews 4:12.
basic.god: God is shown as both cosmically powerful, numbering and naming every star, and intimately compassionate, healing the shattered heart. He sustains all creation, delights in those who fear Him rather than in human strength, and has uniquely revealed His word and statutes to Israel.
basic.crossReferences: Luke 4:18 shows Jesus claiming Isaiah's promise to heal the brokenhearted, echoing verse 3. John 1:1-14 identifies Jesus as the eternal Word, echoing the psalm's picture of God's word running swiftly. Hebrews 4:12 describes the word of God as living and active, matching this psalm's dynamic, effective davar.
basic.oneStory: The LORD who commands the stars by name and commands the weather by word is the same LORD who binds up the brokenhearted and speaks His word to His people, a word fulfilled and embodied in Jesus Christ, the Word made flesh, who heals what is broken and reigns over all creation.

context.literary:
Psalm 147 is a hymn that sounds like a single breath but is built in three movements, each opening with a summons to praise: verse 1, verse 7, and verse 12. Each movement then argues for the summons with a pair of reasons, one from the vast and one from the near. In verses 2 to 6 the LORD rebuilds a city and heals broken people, and in the same stretch He counts and names the stars. In verses 8 to 11 He feeds the grass, the cattle, and the ravens, and has no interest in a cavalry horse. In verses 13 to 20 He bars the gates of Zion and sends out the frost. The psalm will not let the reader keep greatness and tenderness in separate boxes.

The movements are held together by repeated phrases. The verb 'sends' belongs to verses 15 and 18, so that a single word, His word, travels out on each occasion, first to freeze and then to thaw. 'Word' appears again in verse 19 in a different setting, the revelation to Jacob, and by sharing a single word the psalm links the God who speaks to the weather with the God who speaks to Israel. The line about the stars in verse 4 is joined to verse 5 by the idea of number: He 'determines the number of the stars,' and then His understanding 'has no limit,' which in Hebrew is literally 'no number.' The star-counter has an understanding that cannot be counted.

The second movement turns on a sharp negative. After the long list of what God does, verse 10 says what He does not delight in, the horse and the strong legs of a runner, and verse 11 says what He does delight in. The positive and negative sides are set side by side as a proverb would do. The psalm ends with a contrast of its own in verse 20, that other nations do not know His judgments, which turns a hymn about creation into a hymn about a particular people who have been told something.
context.historical:
Verses 2 and 13 give the psalm a likely setting. The LORD 'builds up Jerusalem' and 'gathers the exiles of Israel,' and He 'strengthens the bars of your gates.' That is the language of a city that has been broken and is being put together again, and a number of readers connect it with the return from Babylon and the rebuilding of the walls under Nehemiah. The Fish Gate went up with its 'doors, bolts, and bars,' Nehemiah 3:3, and the wall was finished in fifty-two days, Nehemiah 6:15. Its dedication was a day of singing, Nehemiah 12:27. The psalm may well have been sung at such an occasion, though it does not name one, and the same lines would suit any later occasion when the exiles were gathered. The promise behind verse 2 is old: Moses had said that if Israel were scattered the LORD would gather them from the farthest places, Deuteronomy 30:3-4, and the prophets repeated it, Isaiah 56:8 and Jeremiah 31:8-10.

The weather in verses 16 to 18 is meant for the ear of a people who lived close to the land. Snow was a rarity to many in Judah, though the hills around Jerusalem can see it, and the sense of it falling like wool and frost scattering like ash was vivid and not common. Snow, frost, and hail were treated in Israel as the LORD's storehouse, Job 38:22, and not as a natural cycle running by itself. Verse 14's 'finest wheat' is the phrase used of the best of the harvest in Psalm 81:16, a sign of a blessed land.

In verse 10 the horse and the legs of a man describe the two parts of an ancient army: cavalry and infantry. Israel's law warned that a king must not multiply horses, Deuteronomy 17:16, and the prophets scolded those who trusted in them, Isaiah 31:1. A people who had just been rescued from the failure of the monarchy, and whose city lay in ruins because they had trusted in alliances and armies, would hear verse 10 with a particular edge.
context.canonical:
Psalm 147 draws together lines found across the Old Testament. The building of Jerusalem and the gathering of exiles echo Isaiah 56:8, Jeremiah 31:8-10, and Psalm 102:16, and their roots reach back to Deuteronomy 30:3-4. The healing of the brokenhearted and binding of wounds in verse 3 is the language of Psalm 34:18 and Isaiah 61:1, where the LORD's anointed is sent to bind up the brokenhearted. The stars that He numbers and names are those of Isaiah 40:26, which asks Israel to lift up its eyes and see who made them, and which says that 'not one of them is missing.' Isaiah then draws the conclusion that the God who counts the stars will not forget Jacob, Isaiah 40:27-28, which is the very pairing of the vast and the near that Psalm 147 makes.

The word that runs and does what it is sent to do is a theme in its own right. Psalm 33:6 and 33:9 say that heaven was made by His word, and Psalm 107:20 says that He sent forth His word and healed. Isaiah 55:10-11 compares God's word to rain and snow that come down and do not return without doing what they were sent to do. The psalm reaches the same point from the opposite side: the snow and the word are the same kind of thing, both sent out by the same God.

The New Testament reads the psalm through Jesus. John 1:1-14 introduces the Word who was with God, through whom all things were made, and who became flesh. Hebrews 1:3 says that the Son upholds all things by His powerful word. In the Gospels the wind and the waves obey Him, Mark 4:39-41, in the way the winds and waters obey the word in verse 18. The hunger of the ravens in verse 9 is taken up in the Sermon on the Mount, where Jesus says that the heavenly Father feeds the birds of the air, Matthew 6:26, and, in Luke 12:24, the ravens by name. The line about God's pleasure in those who fear Him is echoed in Isaiah 66:2.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The psalmist meant his hearers to leave with a larger and a smaller God than they came with, and to see that both are the same. They had stood in a city of rubble and watched the work of rebuilding. The temptation in such a time is to assume that the God of the stars is too busy for a broken city, or that the God who tends a broken heart is too small to govern the weather. The psalm does not argue against either mistake. It lays the facts out side by side until the mistakes dissolve: the One who numbers the stars is the One who binds up wounds, and the same verb of care covers both.

He also meant them to hear something about their own position. Israel is the people to whom the word has been spoken, verses 19 and 20, and this is a gift that carries responsibility, since a word that is declared is meant to be kept. The lines about strength in verses 10 and 11 teach the community where its safety lies. A rebuilt city with strong gates might begin to trust the gates, and a restored people might begin to trust the army. The psalm says that God's delight is in those who fear Him and hope in His loving devotion, so that what the community has to offer Him is trust, not strength.

Above all, the author wanted the praise itself to be seen as fitting. Verse 1 calls it good, pleasant, and lovely, three words that treat praise as a pleasure and not as a duty extracted from people. The hearers are invited to enjoy their God.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The psalm mostly describes God and commands praise, and almost all of its application comes from the way the description is set out. It does not prescribe that believers should rebuild city walls, count stars, or keep a particular festival. The details of the rebuilding of Jerusalem describe what God did for Israel at a particular time, and the claim of verse 20 that He has done this for no other nation is a statement of what He did in history, not a standing licence to look down on others.

What is meant to carry forward is a pattern of trust. Because the God who numbers the stars also heals the brokenhearted, a believer can bring both a large and a small trouble to Him without apologising for either, as Peter later says, 'Cast all your anxiety on Him, because He cares for you,' 1 Peter 5:7. Verses 10 and 11 give a caution against a modern form of the horse and the runner's legs: reliance on money, technology, and strength. Using horses and runners is not wrong, since the psalm does not forbid armies or athletes, but trusting them for ultimate security is. The psalm also teaches that wounds are a place for care, and that no one should take 'He heals the brokenhearted' as a reason for the church to leave the work to God alone. The people of God are called to bind wounds as their Lord does, Luke 10:34.

debates.question: How are the 'snow like wool' and 'word' of verses 15 to 18 meant to relate to the word given to Jacob in verse 19?

views.label: A parallel between creation and revelation
views.case: The same word and the same verb of sending appear in both parts, and the psalm intends the reader to connect them. The God who commands the snow and the frost by a word is the One who speaks His statutes to Israel, so that the two words are of the same kind and have the same power. Psalm 19, which moves from the heavens to the law, follows the same pattern.

views.label: A contrast between the general and the particular
views.case: Others read verse 19 as the turn that sets Israel apart from the rest of creation. The weather obeys the word without understanding it, whereas Israel is addressed and expected to understand and keep it. The point is the privilege of being spoken to, and the contrast, in verse 20, is with nations that do not know His judgments.

debates.bearing: The two readings can be held together. The psalm treats the word as one thing that acts on nature by commanding it and on a people by teaching them. The difference between the two lies in the response expected: the frost simply obeys, and Israel is meant to obey knowingly.

debates.question: Is the psalm tied to the return from exile and Nehemiah's wall?

views.label: Yes, composed for the rebuilding
views.case: The building up of Jerusalem, the gathering of exiles, and the strengthening of the gates fit the days of Ezra and Nehemiah closely. The psalm would then have been sung as the city was restored.

views.label: A general hymn that could be used then and since
views.case: The psalm has no title, and its wording is general enough to have been written earlier, for example in the days of Hezekiah, and to have been adopted for later rebuilding. The language of gathering the outcasts is a standing promise, not necessarily a report.

debates.bearing: Nothing in the interpretation hangs on the date. In either case the psalm presents the rebuilding of a broken city as the work of the One who also names the stars, and it invites any community that is being put back together to sing it.

study.originalLanguages:
Verse 3 says that the LORD heals the brokenhearted. The Hebrew describes people who are 'broken of heart,' from the root shabar, to break, the same root that appears in Psalm 34:18 and Isaiah 61:1. The word for heart in these phrases is the seat of will and thought as well as of feeling, so the broken are people whose whole inner life has been fractured. The verb for 'heals' is rapha, the root behind the title the LORD takes in Exodus 15:26, 'I am the LORD, who heals you.' The binding of wounds uses chabash, the verb of wrapping a wound, found in Isaiah 61:1 where the anointed one is sent to bind up the brokenhearted and in Ezekiel 34:4, where the shepherds failed to do it. The image is of a physician at work and not of a distant comforter.

Verse 4 makes a strong claim with two verbs. The LORD 'determines' the number, using the verb of counting, and He 'calls' each by name. In the ancient world, to name something was to exercise authority over it and to know it, and Isaiah 40:26 makes the same point. The psalm then sets the verb 'to count' beside the noun for number in verse 5, where His understanding has no number. The Hebrew for understanding in that line is tevunah, a word of discernment and skill that is used of the craftsmen who built the tabernacle and of wisdom in Proverbs 3:19-20, where the LORD founded the earth by understanding.

Verse 6 says that the LORD 'sustains' the humble. The verb is the one used in Psalm 146:9, where He sustains the fatherless and widow, and a reader who has just come from the previous psalm hears the echo. The 'humble' are the anawim, the poor and lowly who depend on God, a term that is used in the Psalms of those who look to Him for help. The wicked, in contrast, are cast to the ground, and the same ground is the one where the humble stand upright.

The 'word' of verses 15, 18, and 19 is davar, and the psalm gives it three jobs. It runs, 'swiftly,' as if it were a messenger. It melts the snow, and it is declared to Jacob. The verb in verse 19, 'declares,' is a participle of nagad, the verb of telling openly, and it is the same word used of the proclamation of a message.

The word 'finest' in 'finest wheat' translates a Hebrew word for fat, chelev, that stands for the best portion, as in Psalm 81:16. In verse 11 the word 'hope' is a participle of yachal, to wait, and the 'loving devotion' is chesed, the covenant love of the LORD, so that the LORD is pleased with those who wait for His loyal love.

In the Septuagint and Latin Psalters, this psalm is split into two, so that English verses 1 to 11 are Psalm 146 and verses 12 to 20 are Psalm 147. The division has some natural sense, since the third movement opens with its own call to Jerusalem.

typology.type: The LORD who builds up Jerusalem and gathers the exiles, verse 2
typology.fulfillment: The rebuilt city of Ezra and Nehemiah is a real fulfilment of the promise to bring the scattered back, Deuteronomy 30:3-4. But the prophets looked for something larger, a gathering of the dispersed that included others besides those already gathered, Isaiah 56:8. Jesus speaks of gathering the children of Jerusalem as a hen gathers her chicks, Matthew 23:37, and He dies, in John's account, to gather into one the scattered children of God, John 11:51-52. The church is called a building in which God lives, Ephesians 2:19-22, and the writer of Hebrews speaks of the heavenly Jerusalem, Hebrews 12:22. The type falls short of the end, since the rebuilt city was soon conquered again and the true city waits for the day when it comes down from heaven, Revelation 21:2.

typology.type: The LORD who binds up the broken, verse 3
typology.fulfillment: The healer of Israel's wounds is promised again as the anointed Servant who binds up the brokenhearted, Isaiah 61:1. Jesus reads those words as His own mission, Luke 4:18, and acts on them, touching lepers and raising the bent woman in the synagogue, Luke 13:10-13. The escalation is that the physician carries the wound Himself, for Isaiah says that by His stripes we are healed, Isaiah 53:5, and Peter applies the line to the cross, 1 Peter 2:24. The type is incomplete because brokenness remains in this age, and the full healing, when God wipes away every tear, is still to come, Revelation 21:4.

typology.type: The word sent out that does what it is sent to do, verses 15 and 18
typology.fulfillment: The word of the LORD that runs swiftly and accomplishes His purpose, as Isaiah 55:11 says, points toward the Word who is a person. John 1:14 says that the Word became flesh and made His dwelling among us. Where the word of the psalm commanded frost and wind, the Gospels show the incarnate Word commanding the wind and sea, Mark 4:39. Hebrews 1:3 says that He upholds all things by His powerful word. The correspondence is real because the New Testament says the Son is the agent of creation, John 1:3, but the type is not a direct prophecy. The psalm speaks of the spoken word of God, and the New Testament shows how fully that word is gathered into Christ.

typology.type: The word declared to Jacob, verse 19
typology.fulfillment: Israel was given statutes and judgments that no other nation received, Deuteronomy 4:7-8, and Paul says that they were entrusted with the very words of God, Romans 3:2. Jesus fulfils this by being the one to whom the law and prophets pointed, Luke 24:44, and Hebrews opens by saying that God who spoke through the prophets has in these last days spoken by His Son, Hebrews 1:1-2. The pattern also widens. The word that was once declared only to Jacob is carried to the nations, Matthew 28:19, and Paul says that those who were far off have been brought near, Ephesians 2:13. The limit of the type is verse 20 itself, which belongs to the time before that sending.

study.christ:
The psalm leads to Christ first by the word. The line that runs through verses 15 to 19 is that the LORD's word is a swift and effective thing, and the same word is spoken to Jacob. The Gospel of John opens by placing a person at the centre of that idea: the Word who was with God, who was God, through whom all things were made, John 1:1-3, and who 'became flesh and made His dwelling among us,' John 1:14. The wind and sea that obey His word in verse 18 are the wind and sea that obey Jesus in the boat, to the astonishment of the disciples, who ask who this is, Mark 4:41. The writer of Hebrews says that the Son upholds all things by His powerful word, Hebrews 1:3. The psalmist did not know the Son by name, yet the pattern he describes is the pattern the apostles recognised: the word that governs nature and speaks to the covenant people is one and the same, and it has come in person.

It leads to Christ by the healing of the brokenhearted. The Spirit-anointed Servant of Isaiah 61:1 is sent to bind up the brokenhearted, and when Jesus stands in the Nazareth synagogue, He closes the scroll and says that it is fulfilled that day, Luke 4:18-21. The story of His ministry bears it out. A leper comes on his knees and Jesus, moved with compassion, touches him, Mark 1:41. A woman bent over for eighteen years is called over and set free, Luke 13:10-13. The one who calls stars by name also calls ordinary people by name, as the shepherd does his sheep, John 10:3. He is both the great God of verses 4 and 5 and the near God of verse 3.

It leads to Christ by the gathering. The LORD 'gathers the exiles of Israel,' and Jesus describes His own longing to gather Jerusalem's children, Matthew 23:37. John says that He was to die for the nation, and for the scattered children of God, to bring them together as one, John 11:51-52. The prophets said that others besides those already gathered would be brought in, Isaiah 56:8, and in Christ the nations are included, so that the people once far off are brought near, Ephesians 2:13.

It leads to Christ by the contrast about strength. The horse and the strong legs cannot please God. Yet the Messiah of the prophets comes 'humble and riding on a donkey,' Zechariah 9:9, not on a warhorse, and He refuses to call down legions, Matthew 26:53. The power that the psalm puts into God's word is the power Jesus uses: He speaks, and the sick are healed and the dead rise. He is pleased by those who fear Him and hope in the chesed that comes in person.

A caution keeps the reading honest. Psalm 147 is not a prophecy about Jesus in so many words, and the snow and ashes of verse 16 are not codes for His life. The psalm is a hymn to the LORD, and the claim of the New Testament is that what the psalm says of the LORD is true of the Son because He is the LORD come among us. The point of contact is the shared action of word and healing.
study.god:
The psalm gives us a God of two scales, and it does so without apology. On the large scale, He 'determines the number of the stars' and calls each by name, verse 4. He covers the sky with clouds, prepares rain, makes the hills green, spreads snow and frost, and commands the winds, verses 8 and 15 to 18. The psalm piles up these works to say that nothing in the physical world operates apart from Him. This is a God whose understanding 'has no limit,' verse 5, so that nothing, large or small, escapes His knowledge. On the small scale, He heals the brokenhearted, binds up their wounds, and feeds the young ravens when they call, verses 3 and 9. The word 'call' in verse 9 gives the ravens a voice, as though their cries were prayers He hears. The two scales are not in tension for the psalmist, and they are part of the same greatness.

He is sovereign over nature without being a part of it. The snow is His, and the frost is His. When the psalm asks, 'Who can withstand His icy blast?' the answer is plain, and the question prepares us for the next verse, which says that He sends forth His word and the ice melts. The same command that freezes thaws, and nothing in the weather is out of His control.

He is a provider. Verse 9 and verse 14 describe a God who feeds animals and who fills a people with the finest wheat. His provision is not stingy. The language of 'fills' suggests abundance, and the peace at the borders is also His gift, so that security and daily bread come from the same hand.

He is a God who prefers the humble. The wicked are cast to the ground and the humble are sustained, verse 6. He does not delight in the strength of horse or man, verse 10. His delight rests on those who fear Him and who hope in His loving devotion, verse 11. The object of His pleasure is a posture of trust and not a display of strength, which fits what Isaiah 66:2 says about the one He esteems.

He is a God who speaks. The psalm gives weight to His word, which runs, melts, and is declared. He has told Israel what He is like and what He asks, and the statutes and judgments of verse 19 are a sign of nearness, as Deuteronomy 4:7 says: no other nation has a god so near. The word of God is a mark of His grace.

For worship, the psalm teaches that praise is fitting. It is 'good,' 'pleasant,' and 'lovely,' verse 1. The right response to a God who is at once vast and near is to sing, with thanksgiving and music, verse 7. Worship in this psalm is not a mood to be summoned but a reply to what He has done, and it grows by looking at the stars and at one's own wounds, and seeing the same hand.

crossReferences.note: Isaiah asks Israel to lift up its eyes and see who created the stars, the One who leads them forth by number and calls each by name. It is the closest parallel to verse 4, and Isaiah uses it for the same reason, to assure scattered people that they have not been forgotten.

The anointed one is sent to bind up the brokenhearted. The Hebrew phrase and the idea of binding are the ones of verse 3, so that the psalm's healing of the heart becomes the commission of the Servant who is to come.

The LORD is near to the brokenhearted and saves the crushed in spirit. It states in a single line the nearness that Psalm 147:3 describes in action, and it shows that the care for the broken was already a settled fact of Israel's worship.

The previous psalm says that the LORD sustains the fatherless and widow, using the same verb that Psalm 147:6 uses for the humble. The two psalms stand together at the end of the Psalter, and reading them in turn shows that the same care runs through both.
Moses promises that if Israel is scattered to the farthest places, the LORD will gather them from there. It is the older promise behind verse 2, and the psalm reports that God keeps it.

The dedication of Jerusalem's wall was kept with thanksgiving and singing, with cymbals, harps, and lyres. It gives a picture of the kind of occasion in which a psalm like this one would be sung, and the link to verse 13's strengthened gates is natural, though the psalm does not name the event.

God's word is compared to rain and snow that come down and do not return without doing what He pleases. The comparison is the mirror image of Psalm 147:15-18, where snow and word travel together, and each text reads the other as the same God at work.

No king is saved by a great army and a horse is a vain hope, while the eyes of the LORD are on those who fear Him and hope in His loving devotion. It states the lesson of verses 10 and 11 almost in the same words, which shows how deeply the teaching was held.

Jesus says that the birds neither sow nor reap, yet the heavenly Father feeds them, and that His hearers are worth more than they. He draws on the world of verse 9 and uses it as a reason against anxiety.

The Word was with God, was God, and made all things. John gathers up the psalm's picture of a word that makes and rules and names the Word as a person, which is why the Gospel and the psalm can be read together.

God who once spoke through the prophets has in these last days spoken by His Son, who upholds all things by His powerful word. It matches verse 19, where God declares His word to Jacob, with its fullest declaration, and verse 15, where the word rules creation, with the One who rules by it.

The new Jerusalem comes down from God, and He wipes away every tear. The rebuilt city and the healed heart of the psalm arrive together here, and the exiles who were gathered in verse 2 become a people who live with God for good.

study.oneStory:
This psalm sits in the story at the point of return. Israel had been scattered because it trusted in its own strength and forgot the word it was given, and the prophets had promised that the LORD would gather the scattered and rebuild the ruins, Isaiah 52:9 and Jeremiah 31:8-10. When some of the exiles came back, this psalm gave voice to what they saw: a city rising, a people regathered, the LORD at work on the broken. It answers the question of whether the God who judged is still the God who restores.

It reaches back to creation. The stars that the LORD numbers are the stars of Genesis 1:16, and the story begins with a God who speaks and things are made, Genesis 1:3. Abraham was told to count the stars if he could, and promised descendants as numerous, Genesis 15:5, which means that the God who numbers the stars also keeps the promise made under them. The 'word' that runs swiftly in verse 15 is the voice that said 'Let there be light.' Psalm 147 says that the God of creation did not retire after the seventh day, and that the same word sustains the world.

It also looks forward, because the promise of restoration was larger than the return. The rebuilt city of Nehemiah's day had walls but no king on David's throne, and prophets spoke of a greater gathering. The story arrives at the one who says to the crowd, 'Come to Me, all you who are weary,' Matthew 11:28, who heals the brokenhearted, who commands wind and sea, and who gathers from every nation, John 11:51-52. The Word who made the stars has come as a Man who can be touched. His people are then sent out to carry the word that was once declared to Jacob alone, so that what was exclusive in verse 20 becomes open to all, Matthew 28:19-20.

The story ends with the rebuilt city made perfect. Revelation 21:2 sees the holy city, the new Jerusalem, coming down out of heaven from God, and its gates are never shut, Revelation 21:25. The bars that the LORD strengthened in the psalm are no longer needed, because nothing unclean enters and no enemy waits outside. The nations walk by its light, Revelation 21:24, and the Lord who healed the brokenhearted wipes every tear from their eyes, Revelation 21:4. The tree of life, withheld in Genesis 3, stands in the street, and its leaves are for the healing of the nations, Revelation 22:2. The psalm's three themes of rebuilt city, healed heart, and spoken word all arrive at once: the city is the people, the healing is complete, and the Word is the Lamb on the throne, with His people seeing His face, Revelation 22:3-4.

sermon.title: Singing, Suffering, and Scripture: How God Keeps Us Through Song
sermon.why: Piper works from Psalm 147:1's call to sing praises that are good and fitting, tracing three ways singing relates to suffering, stopped by it, sustaining through it, and following after it forever, showing how this psalm's summons to praise meets believers in real affliction.

quiz.q: According to verses 2-3, what does the LORD do for Jerusalem and the brokenhearted?

options.text: He builds up Jerusalem, gathers the exiles, heals the brokenhearted, and binds up their wounds.
options.note: These verses pair national restoration with personal, intimate healing.

options.text: He rebukes Jerusalem for her sins and scatters her people further.
options.note: The opposite is described; the LORD gathers and restores, He does not scatter here.

options.text: He ignores Jerusalem until a distant future.
options.note: The psalm describes present, active restoration, not future neglect.

options.text: He rebuilds Jerusalem but leaves the people's wounds untouched.
options.note: The text explicitly adds that He also heals the brokenhearted, not only the city.

quiz.q: What does verse 4 say the LORD does with the stars?

options.text: He determines their number and calls each one by name.
options.note: This pictures God's intimate, personal knowledge of the vastness of the cosmos.

options.text: He merely watches them from a distance.
options.note: The verse describes active naming and numbering, not distant observation.

options.text: He leaves their number a mystery even to Himself.
options.note: The verse says the opposite, that He determines their number precisely.

options.text: He created them but no longer takes notice of them.
options.note: The verse emphasizes His ongoing, personal attention, calling each star by name.

quiz.q: In what does the LORD delight, according to verses 10-11?

options.text: Not in the strength of horse or man, but in those who fear Him and hope in His loving devotion.
options.note: The LORD's pleasure rests on reverent trust, not on impressive human or animal strength.

options.text: In powerful armies and swift warhorses.
options.note: Verse 10 explicitly denies that God delights in these things.

options.text: In wealth and impressive human achievement.
options.note: The passage contrasts strength with humble, trusting fear of the LORD, not wealth specifically.

options.text: Primarily in outward religious performance.
options.note: The emphasis falls on inward fear of the LORD and hope in His hesed, not mere outward performance.

quiz.q: What is unique about Israel's relationship to God, according to verses 19-20?

options.text: He has declared His word and statutes to Jacob as He has done for no other nation.
options.note: The psalm closes by naming this covenant revelation as Israel's particular privilege.

options.text: Israel earned this word through perfect obedience.
options.note: The text presents this as a gift of revelation, not a reward for perfect obedience.

options.text: Every nation received the same revelation equally.
options.note: The verse explicitly says the opposite, He has not done this for other nations.

options.text: Israel alone among all peoples will ever know God.
options.note: The verse describes a historical, covenantal uniqueness, which the New Testament shows extending to all nations in Christ.

quiz.q: How does this psalm's picture of God's word connect to the New Testament?

options.text: God's word running swiftly points to the Word made flesh, John 1:14, and the living, active word of God, Hebrews 4:12.
options.note: The psalm's dynamic, effective davar anticipates the incarnate and living Word of the New Testament.

options.text: It only refers to the weather patterns described in the psalm.
options.note: The weather imagery is real, but Scripture develops this word imagery further toward Christ.

options.text: It has no meaningful New Testament connection.
options.note: John's Gospel draws directly on this kind of Old Testament word theology.

options.text: It predicts a specific future political event.
options.note: The connection is theological, God's living word, rather than a specific political prediction.

questions: The LORD heals the brokenhearted and binds up their wounds, verse 3. What wound are you carrying that needs His healing touch today?
He numbers and names every star, yet stoops to the brokenhearted. How does holding those two truths together, God's vastness and His nearness, change how you pray?
The LORD delights not in human strength but in those who fear Him and hope in His loving devotion, verses 10-11. Where are you tempted to trust your own strength rather than His steadfast love?
God declares His word uniquely to His people, verses 19-20. How does having God's word in Scripture shape the way you approach a decision you are facing this week?
This psalm calls for thanksgiving and music, verse 7. What specific thing from this past week deserves a fresh song of thanks to God?

translationNotes.note: Hallelujah renders halelu-yah, opening and closing this psalm and framing the Psalter's final movement of praise.
Brokenhearted renders nishberei lev, literally shattered of heart, stressing inward, emotional devastation rather than only physical affliction.
Pebbles, also rendered crumbs or morsels, describes hail falling like small, hard pieces, an image of God's word made visible in weather.
